en: to compare two things that differ in essential respects
to evaluate subjects with different conditions, assumptions, or categories by the same standard
to place data or results lacking a common measurement basis side by side
to draw a conclusion while ignoring material differences
to make a comparison that is unfair, misleading, or not meaningful

nuance.ja: compare apples and oranges は、比較対象の性質・条件・目的などが本質的に異なるため、そのまま同じ基準で評価するのは不適切だと指摘する表現である。例えば、従業員10人の新興企業の総売上高と、世界的企業の総売上高だけを比較して効率を評価すれば、規模・市場・事業構造を無視した apples-to-oranges comparison になり得る。ただし、リンゴとオレンジにも価格・重量・栄養価など比較可能な側面があるように、この慣用句は「両者を一切比較できない」と論理的に断定するものではない。問題は、議論の目的に適した共通基準があるか、重要な相違を調整しているかである。比較を単に避けるのではなく、条件をそろえて compare apples to apples「同種のものを比較する」ことが重要となる。
nuance.en: Compare apples and oranges criticizes an attempt to evaluate two subjects by the same standard even though their nature, conditions, or purposes differ materially. For example, comparing only the total revenue of a ten-person startup with that of a global corporation to assess efficiency may ignore scale, markets, and business structure and therefore become an apples-to-oranges comparison. The idiom does not logically establish that no comparison at all is possible; apples and oranges can themselves be compared by price, weight, or nutritional value. The relevant question is whether the analysis uses a common basis appropriate to its purpose and adjusts for material differences. A sounder analysis attempts to compare apples to apples by aligning definitions, conditions, and measurement methods.

ja: compare apples and oranges：本質的条件の異なる対象を同じ基準で不適切に比較する。
compare apples to apples：同種・同条件の対象を公平な基準で比較する。

etymology.ja: compare apples and oranges は、リンゴとオレンジがどちらも果物ではあるものの、味・形・性質などが異なることを利用した比喩表現である。異なる種類の物を同一基準で扱う不合理さを示す言い回しとして、20世紀のアメリカ英語で広く定着した。英語では以前から apples and pears など、異なる果物を並べて不適切な比較を示す類似表現が存在した。現在では compare apples to oranges、compare apples with oranges、comparing apples and oranges などの形で、議論・統計・ビジネス分析における比較条件の不一致を指摘する。
etymology.en: Compare apples and oranges uses the fact that apples and oranges, although both fruit, differ in taste, appearance, and other characteristics. It became widely established in twentieth-century American English as a metaphor for the unreasonable use of one standard to evaluate unlike things. English had earlier used other pairs of different fruit, including apples and pears, in similar comparisons. The modern forms compare apples to oranges, compare apples with oranges, and comparing apples and oranges commonly identify mismatched conditions in argument, statistics, and business analysis.

usage.meaning: The idiom means offering something valuable to people who cannot or will not recognize its worth.
usage.verb: Cast has the same base, past, and past-participle form in this expression: cast, cast, cast.
usage.fixed_nouns: Pearls and swine normally remain plural. Swine is an old or formal collective and plural word for pigs.
usage.variant: Throw pearls before swine is a modernized variant, but cast pearls before swine preserves the traditional biblical wording.
usage.scope: The valuable thing may be advice, knowledge, art, generosity, effort, or an opportunity rather than a physical object.
usage.evaluation: The phrase strongly disparages the recipients by comparing them to pigs and may also suggest arrogance on the speaker’s part.
usage.frequency: It is widely recognizable but relatively rare in ordinary modern conversation.
usage.register: It sounds literary, biblical, or deliberately dramatic. Waste something on an unappreciative audience is more neutral.

ja: 価値を理解できない人に貴重な物・知識を与える

受け手に活用する能力や意思がないのに、価値ある機会を提供する
「豚に真珠」に当たる、無駄で報われない行為をする

en: to offer something valuable to people incapable of appreciating its worth
to waste excellent advice, knowledge, art, or effort on an ungrateful audience
to provide a valuable opportunity to recipients unable or unwilling to use it
to perform an unrewarding act comparable to giving pearls to pigs
to characterize the recipients contemptuously as lacking judgment or appreciation

nuance.ja: cast pearls before swine は、日本語の「豚に真珠」とほぼ同じく、価値の分からない相手に貴重なものを与えても無駄であることを表す。pearls は知識・助言・芸術・努力・機会などの価値あるもの、swine はその価値を認識しない受け手の比喩である。ただし、単に提案が受け入れられなかったというだけではなく、受け手に理解力・教養・感謝がないと断定する強い軽蔑を含む。このため、他人について使うと侮辱的で、話者自身の尊大さを印象づけることもある。現代の職場では、They did not appreciate the advice. や The information was not suited to the audience. のような中立的な表現の方が安全である。
nuance.en: Cast pearls before swine closely corresponds to the Japanese proverb 豚に真珠 and describes the futility of giving something valuable to recipients who do not appreciate it. The pearls metaphorically represent knowledge, advice, art, effort, or opportunity, while the swine represent those who fail to recognize its value. The expression says more than that a proposal was rejected: it strongly judges the recipients as lacking understanding, refinement, or gratitude. It can therefore be insulting and may also make the speaker appear arrogant. In a modern workplace, neutral language such as They did not appreciate the advice or The information was not suited to the audience is generally safer.

etymology.ja: cast pearls before swine は『新約聖書』マタイによる福音書7章6節の表現に由来する。伝統的な英訳では、神聖なものを犬に与えず、真珠を豚の前に投げてはならないと説かれる。古代において真珠は非常に価値の高い宝石である一方、豚はその価値を理解せず踏みつける存在として対比された。宗教的文脈を離れた後も、価値を認識できない相手に貴重な物を与えるという比喩として定着した。日本語の「豚に真珠」も、この聖書表現を背景とする。
etymology.en: Cast pearls before swine derives from Matthew 7:6 in the New Testament. In traditional English translations, the passage warns against giving what is holy to dogs or casting pearls before swine. Pearls were extremely valuable objects in the ancient world, whereas pigs were presented as incapable of recognizing their value and likely to trample them. Outside its original religious context, the expression became a general metaphor for offering something valuable to recipients unable to appreciate it. The Japanese proverb 豚に真珠 has the same biblical background.

usage.of: Appreciative most commonly takes of for the thing valued: appreciative of your assistance.
usage.person: Toward or towards may introduce the person receiving the positive attitude, but grateful to someone is often more natural for direct gratitude.
usage.that_clause: Be appreciative that introduces the fact causing gratitude: We are appreciative that you responded promptly.
usage.gratitude: When referring to help or kindness, appreciative means feeling and showing gratitude.
usage.recognition: It can also mean recognizing and understanding the quality or value of art, skill, effort, food, or another experience.
usage.expression: An appreciative smile, nod, or audience visibly communicates approval or enjoyment.
usage.comparison: More appreciative and most appreciative are standard.
usage.register: It is natural in polite, professional, and general English, though grateful is often warmer and more personal.

en: feeling or showing gratitude for help, kindness, or consideration
recognizing and properly valuing an object, action, or effort
capable of understanding and enjoying the quality of art, skill, food, or another experience
for an expression or response, communicating gratitude, admiration, or pleasure
for an audience, responding favorably to a presentation or performance

nuance.ja: appreciative には、主に「感謝している」と「価値を理解して高く評価している」という二つの側面がある。I’m appreciative of your help. は援助への感謝を表すが、I’m grateful for your help. の方が日常会話ではより自然で温かく響く場合が多い。一方、an appreciative audience は単に礼を言う聴衆ではなく、演技・講演などの良さを理解して好意的に反応する聴衆である。appreciative of art なら、芸術の価値や細部を味わう能力・姿勢を示す。感謝や評価を内心で感じるだけでなく、笑顔・うなずき・拍手などでそれを示している含みを持つことも多い。appreciative of が標準的であり、appreciative for より自然である。
nuance.en: Appreciative has two closely connected aspects: feeling grateful and recognizing something’s value or quality. I’m appreciative of your help expresses gratitude, although I’m grateful for your help is often warmer and more natural in everyday conversation. An appreciative audience is not merely an audience saying thank you; it understands and responds favorably to the quality of a performance or presentation. Someone appreciative of art is able and willing to recognize and enjoy its value or detail. The adjective often suggests that gratitude or approval is visibly communicated through a smile, nod, applause, or comment. Appreciative of is the standard construction and is normally more natural than appreciative for.

ja: appreciative：感謝を示す、または物事の価値・良さを理解して評価する。
grateful：人から受けた助け・親切・幸運について心から感謝している。

unappreciative：受けた恩恵や物事の価値を認めず、感謝を示さない。
en: appreciative means feeling gratitude or recognizing and responding to quality or value.
grateful means sincerely thankful for help, kindness, or fortunate circumstances.
thankful means pleased and relieved about a benefit received or a bad outcome avoided.
admiring means showing approval and respect for someone’s ability, character, or work.
receptive means willing to receive and consider an idea, proposal, or information.
complimentary means expressing praise or, in another sense, provided free of charge.
discerning means capable of recognizing subtle differences in quality or value.
unappreciative means failing to recognize value or show gratitude for a benefit.

etymology.ja: appreciative は動詞 appreciate に形容詞接尾辞 -ive が付いて成立した。appreciate は後期ラテン語 appretiare「価値を定める、評価する」に由来し、ad-「～へ」と pretium「価格・価値」から成る。もともとは物の金銭的価値を見積もることを表したが、そこから価値・品質・重要性を正しく認識する意味、さらに受けた親切や利益の価値を認めて感謝する意味へ発展した。appreciation、appreciatively、appreciative も同じ語族に属する。
etymology.en: Appreciative was formed from appreciate with the adjective-forming suffix -ive. Appreciate derives from Late Latin appretiare, to set a value on, formed from ad-, toward, and pretium, price or value. It originally concerned estimating monetary value, then developed the broader meaning of properly recognizing quality, importance, or worth. Recognizing the value of kindness or a benefit subsequently produced the sense of gratitude. Appreciation, appreciatively, and appreciative belong to the same word family.

usage.evaluation: The word is generally positive, but being excessively receptive may imply insufficient critical judgment.

nuance.ja: receptive は、外部から来る考え・提案・感情・刺激などを拒まず、受け入れる用意があることを表す。be receptive to feedback なら、フィードバックに必ず同意するという意味ではなく、まず耳を傾け、真剣に検討する姿勢があることを示す。open-minded と近いが、open-minded は固定観念にとらわれず幅広い考えを検討する一般的な性格・態度を表し、receptive は特定の提案・影響・働きかけを受け入れやすい状態に焦点を置く。an appreciative audience が発表の価値を理解して好意的に評価する聴衆であるのに対し、a receptive audience は内容を受け入れ、話を聞く用意のある聴衆である。通常は肯定的だが、何でも無批判に受け入れることまでは意味しない。
nuance.en: Receptive describes readiness to receive an idea, proposal, emotion, stimulus, or other external influence instead of rejecting it immediately. Be receptive to feedback does not mean automatically agreeing with the feedback; it means being willing to listen and consider it seriously. Open-minded is close but generally describes a broader freedom from fixed assumptions, whereas receptive focuses on readiness to respond to a particular suggestion or influence. An appreciative audience recognizes and favorably evaluates the quality of a presentation, while a receptive audience is willing to listen to and accept its message. The adjective is normally positive but does not inherently mean accepting everything without critical judgment.

ja: receptive：考え・提案・助言・影響などを受け入れて検討する用意がある。

open-minded means willing to evaluate differing ideas fairly without fixed assumptions.

appreciative means showing gratitude or recognizing and valuing quality.

etymology.ja: receptive は、フランス語 réceptif や中世ラテン語 receptivus を経て、ラテン語 recipere「受け取る、受け入れる」に由来する。recipere は re-「戻って」と capere「取る」から成る。もともとは物・刺激などを受け取る能力を表し、そこから考え・提案・影響を心理的に受け入れる用意があるという意味へ広がった。receive、reception、recipient、receptacle なども同じラテン語系統に属する。名詞 receptivity は、物理的・生物学的な受容性と、心理的な受容力の両方に使われる。
etymology.en: Receptive came through French réceptif and Medieval Latin receptivus from Latin recipere, meaning to receive or take in. Recipere was formed from re-, back, and capere, to take. The adjective initially concerned the capacity to receive an object or stimulus and subsequently developed the psychological sense of being willing to accept an idea, proposal, or influence. Receive, reception, recipient, and receptacle belong to the same Latin family. The noun receptivity can describe both physical or biological capacity and psychological openness.

usage.meaning: Banal describes something unoriginal, predictable, and uninteresting because it has been said, written, or experienced too often.
usage.objects: It commonly modifies comments, ideas, observations, dialogue, plots, phrases, routines, and details.
usage.evaluation: The word is normally critical and suggests both familiarity and a lack of intellectual, artistic, or emotional freshness.
usage.people: It more naturally describes what a person says or produces than the person directly.
usage.comparison: More banal and most banal are standard.
usage.pronunciation: Several pronunciations occur in American English. The second-syllable-stressed /bəˈnæl/ is common; British English commonly uses /bəˈnɑːl/.
usage.noun: A banality is a commonplace, unoriginal statement or feature. Banalities often refers to conventional remarks.
usage.register: Banal is more formal and intellectually critical than everyday words such as boring or ordinary.

en: so commonplace that it lacks originality or freshness
made uninteresting through excessive repetition
predictable and lacking anything distinctive or stimulating

nuance.ja: banal は、単に広く見られるというだけでなく、使い古され、独創性や知的刺激を失っているという批判を含む。a banal comment は、内容が間違っているとは限らないが、誰でも言える月並みな発言である。ordinary は価値判断を伴わず「普通の」と述べられるのに対し、banal は退屈・浅薄・陳腐という否定的評価を示す。trivial は重要性が低いこと、clichéd は表現や発想が使い古されていることを特に強調する。芸術・文学・学術的議論でよく使われるが、日常的な出来事について the banal details of everyday life のように用いると、平凡で目立たない側面を表すこともある。
nuance.en: Banal does not merely mean common. It critically suggests that something has become stale and has lost originality or intellectual interest through familiarity or repetition. A banal comment need not be false, but it is predictable and could have been made by almost anyone. Ordinary can neutrally describe something as normal, whereas banal conveys a negative judgment of dullness, superficiality, or lack of freshness. Trivial particularly emphasizes lack of importance, while clichéd emphasizes an overused form of expression or idea. The word is common in criticism of art, literature, and argument, although the banal details of everyday life can more neutrally identify ordinary and inconspicuous aspects of experience.

etymology.ja: banal はフランス語 banal に由来する。中世フランス語では、領主が ban「布告・支配権」によって住民へ共同使用を命じる製粉所・かまどなどを表し、「共同体全員が使用するもの」という意味を持った。そこから「誰にでも共通の」「普通の」という意味が生まれ、さらに「ありふれて独創性がない」という現在の否定的意味へ発展した。名詞 banality は「陳腐さ」または「月並みな発言」を表す。banal は、ドイツ語 banal、イタリア語 banale、フランス語 banal、スペイン語 banal としてヨーロッパ諸語に広く共有されている。
etymology.en: Banal was borrowed from French banal. In medieval French, it described facilities such as a mill or oven that inhabitants were required to use under a feudal lord’s ban, or legal authority. From the idea of something used by everyone in the community, it developed the meaning common to all or ordinary. This in turn produced the modern negative sense commonplace and lacking originality. The noun banality means either the quality of being banal or a commonplace remark. Cognate forms are widely shared among European languages, including German banal, Italian banale, French banal, and Spanish banal.

usage.ordinary: Mundane commonly describes an ordinary, repetitive, or practical part of daily life.
usage.boring: It often suggests dullness or lack of excitement, though it can neutrally distinguish routine matters from exceptional ones.

en: ordinary and belonging to everyday life
repetitive and lacking excitement or interest
practical and unglamorous rather than exceptional

formally or literarily, belonging to the earthly world rather than a spiritual or heavenly realm

nuance.ja: mundane は、日常生活に属し、特別・劇的・刺激的ではないものを表す。mundane tasks は、掃除・書類整理・データ入力など、必要ではあるが面白みに乏しい日常的作業を指す。boring が話者の主観的な退屈を直接示すのに対し、mundane は対象が反復的・平凡・実務的であることをやや距離を置いて表す。ordinary より「華やかさや新鮮味に欠ける」という含みが強いが、必ずしも強い批判ではない。the mundane details that keep a business running のように、目立たないが必要な事柄を肯定的に捉えることもできる。哲学・宗教・文学では、mundane world が「天上・精神世界に対する現世」を意味する。
nuance.en: Mundane describes something belonging to ordinary life and lacking an exceptional, dramatic, or stimulating quality. Mundane tasks include necessary but unexciting activities such as cleaning, filing documents, and entering data. Boring directly expresses the speaker’s experience of being uninterested, whereas mundane more objectively characterizes something as repetitive, ordinary, or practical. It has a stronger suggestion of lacking glamour or freshness than ordinary, but it is not invariably harsh. In the mundane details that keep a business running, the word may positively acknowledge necessary work that receives little attention. In philosophical, religious, and literary contexts, the mundane world means the earthly realm as opposed to a heavenly or spiritual one.

en: mundane means ordinary, routine, practical, and lacking excitement or glamour.
ordinary means normal and not special and is the most neutral term.

etymology.ja: mundane はフランス語 mondain やラテン語 mundanus「世界の、世俗の」を経て、ラテン語 mundus「世界」に由来する。もともとは天上・精神的領域に対する「地上世界に属する」という意味であった。そこから、現世の日常的な事柄、さらに「普通の、平凡で刺激のない」という現在の一般的意味が発達した。同じラテン語 mundus から、フランス語 monde、イタリア語 mondo、スペイン語 mundo などの「世界」を表す語も生まれている。
etymology.en: Mundane comes through French mondain and Latin mundanus, meaning of the world or earthly, from Latin mundus, world. Its original sense concerned belonging to the earthly realm as opposed to a heavenly or spiritual sphere. From earthly affairs, it developed associations with the ordinary matters of daily life and eventually the common modern meaning routine, unexceptional, and lacking excitement. The same Latin noun mundus produced words for world such as French monde, Italian mondo, and Spanish mundo.

nuance.ja: novelty には、①新しさ・新規性、②珍しい物や体験、③新しいために感じられる一時的な面白さ、という主要な意味がある。The novelty soon wore off. なら、最初は新鮮で面白かったが、慣れるにつれて魅力が薄れたという意味である。a novelty item は、実用性より珍しさ・冗談・装飾性を重視した商品を指すことが多い。特許法上の novelty は専門的な「新規性」であり、単に発明が珍しい、独創的、商業的に新しいという意味ではない。一般に、特許請求された発明の全構成が基準となる先行開示から直接かつ明確に把握できる場合、新規性が問題となる。一方、複数の資料を組み合わせた容易想到性の議論は、通常、進歩性・非自明性の問題であり、新規性とは区別される。
nuance.en: Novelty has three principal senses: newness or originality, an unusual object or experience, and the temporary interest created by unfamiliarity. The novelty soon wore off means that something initially seemed exciting but became less appealing through familiarity. A novelty item is commonly sold more for amusement, unusual appearance, or decoration than for serious practical value. In patent law, novelty is a technical requirement and does not merely mean that an invention seems unusual, creative, or commercially new. Broadly, novelty is at issue when all elements of a claimed invention can be derived from a relevant prior disclosure under the applicable standard. An argument based on combining multiple references more commonly concerns inventive step or nonobviousness and should be distinguished from novelty.

etymology.ja: novelty は古フランス語 noveleté「新しさ、新しい物」を経て、ラテン語 novellus「若い、新しい」に由来する。novellus は novus「新しい」の指小形である。英語では当初、新しい状態・新奇な物を広く表し、そこから珍しさによる一時的な魅力や、面白い小物という意味が発達した。特許制度の発展に伴い、発明が既知でないことを表す専門用語としても定着した。novel「新しい、斬新な」と innovation の基礎にある novus も同じラテン語族に属する。小説を意味する novel も、もとは「新しい話」という発想から発達した。
etymology.en: Novelty came through Old French noveleté, meaning newness or a new thing, from Latin novellus, young or new. Novellus was a diminutive of novus, new. In English, novelty initially referred broadly to the condition of being new or to something new and unusual. It subsequently developed the senses of temporary appeal through unfamiliarity and an amusing or unusual object. With the development of patent systems, it became established as the technical term for the requirement that an invention be new. Novel and the Latin base underlying innovation belong to the same word family.

usage.uncountable: Nonobviousness is normally uncountable: establish nonobviousness, not establish a nonobviousness.
usage.american_law: In United States patent law, nonobviousness is the patentability requirement associated with 35 U.S.C. §103.
usage.basic_test: Broadly, the inquiry asks whether the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the legally relevant time.
usage.claim_focus: The analysis concerns the claimed invention as a whole rather than merely asking whether each element was separately known.
usage.evidence: The determination may involve the scope and content of the prior art, differences from the claimed invention, the level of ordinary skill, articulated reasoning, and relevant objective evidence.
usage.novelty: Nonobviousness is distinct from novelty. A claim may be novel because no single prior-art disclosure contains every limitation yet still be obvious in view of the prior art.
usage.international: Inventive step is the usual corresponding expression in many non-U.S. patent systems, but the governing legal tests are not necessarily identical.
usage.spelling: Nonobviousness is commonly written as one word. The statutory heading uses non-obvious subject matter with a hyphen.

nuance.ja: nonobviousness は、一般的な「意外さ」ではなく、主に米国特許法における専門的な特許要件を表す。発明者本人や一般消費者にとって思いつきにくかったかではなく、法的に関連する先行技術を踏まえ、基準時に当該技術分野の通常の知識・技能を持つ仮想的な当業者にとって自明であったかが問題となる。novelty とは別の要件であり、一件の先行資料にクレームの全構成が開示されていなくても、先行技術の教示を組み合わせる十分な理由があり、結果が予測可能であれば、自明と判断される可能性がある。他方、商業的成功・長期間未解決だった必要性・他者の失敗・予想外の結果などは、主張された発明との結び付きが認められる場合、非自明性を裏付ける客観的証拠となり得る。日本・欧州などでは通常「進歩性」inventive step という語を用いるが、法的判断枠組みまで完全に同一とは限らない。
nuance.en: Nonobviousness is not merely the everyday quality of being surprising; it is principally a technical requirement of United States patent law. The question is not whether the invention was difficult for the inventor or an ordinary consumer to conceive. It concerns whether, in view of the legally relevant prior art, the claimed invention would have been obvious at the relevant time to the hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art. It is distinct from novelty. Even when no single reference discloses every claim limitation, the claim may be obvious if the prior art supplies an adequate reason to make a combination or modification with a predictable result. Conversely, commercial success, a long-felt but unresolved need, failure of others, and unexpected results may constitute objective evidence supporting nonobviousness when sufficiently connected to the claimed invention. Many other patent systems use inventive step as the corresponding expression, but their legal tests are not necessarily identical.

objective evidence includes commercial success or unexpected results that may bear on the nonobviousness inquiry.

etymology.ja: nonobviousness は、否定を表す接頭辞 non-、形容詞 obvious、性質を表す接尾辞 -ness から成る。obvious はラテン語 obvius「道に立ちはだかる、すぐ目の前にある」に由来し、ob-「～に向かって」と via「道」から構成される。目の前にあって容易に気付くという意味から、「明白な、自明な」へ発展した。したがって nonobviousness は語構成上「自明でない性質」を意味する。米国特許法では、1952年特許法によって35 U.S.C. §103の見出しと本文に非自明性の考え方が明文化され、特許性を判断する中心的概念となった。
etymology.en: Nonobviousness is formed from the negative prefix non-, the adjective obvious, and the quality-forming suffix -ness. Obvious derives from Latin obvius, standing in the way or readily encountered, formed from ob-, toward, and via, way or road. The idea of something lying directly in one’s path developed into the meaning readily apparent. Nonobviousness therefore literally denotes the quality of not being obvious. In United States patent law, the Patent Act of 1952 codified the nonobviousness concept in 35 U.S.C. §103, making it a central requirement of patentability.

usage.uncountable: Patentability is normally uncountable: assess patentability, not assess a patentability.
usage.meaning: Patentability means the capacity of an invention or claimed subject matter to satisfy the legal requirements for obtaining a patent.
usage.multiple_requirements: The applicable requirements may include eligible subject matter, novelty, inventive step or nonobviousness, utility or industrial applicability, and sufficient disclosure, depending on the jurisdiction and type of patent.
usage.claim_focus: Patentability is generally assessed in relation to the claimed subject matter rather than an invention described only in broad or commercial terms.
usage.eligibility: Patentability is broader than patent eligibility or patentable subject matter, which addresses whether the relevant category of subject matter can receive patent protection.
usage.validity: Patentability concerns whether patent protection should be granted; validity concerns whether an issued patent remains legally enforceable, though the underlying issues may overlap.
usage.search: A patentability search principally investigates prior art relevant to novelty and inventive step or nonobviousness but cannot conclusively guarantee that a patent will be granted.
usage.jurisdiction: Patentability requirements and examination standards vary by jurisdiction, filing date, claim type, and applicable law.

nuance.ja: patentability は「特許性」、すなわち発明またはクレームされた主題が、適用法上の特許要件を満たすかという総合的な概念である。単に技術が新しいという意味ではなく、新規性、進歩性・非自明性、特許適格性、実用性・産業上の利用可能性、開示要件など、法域に応じた複数の問題が関係し得る。patent eligibility は保護対象となり得る主題の種類かを問う、より限定された概念であり、patentability 全体とは同義ではない。また、patentability search は主として関連する先行技術を調べ、新規性や進歩性を予備的に評価するものだが、未公開資料・調査範囲・審査官の判断などがあるため、特許取得を保証するものではない。さらに、特許を取得できることと、その技術を他者の権利を侵害せず実施できることは別問題である。
nuance.en: Patentability is the overall legal capacity of an invention or claimed subject matter to satisfy the requirements for patent protection. It does not merely mean that a technology appears new. Depending on the jurisdiction, relevant questions may include novelty, inventive step or nonobviousness, patent eligibility, utility or industrial applicability, and disclosure requirements. Patent eligibility is narrower: it asks whether the subject matter belongs to a category capable of receiving patent protection and is therefore not synonymous with patentability as a whole. A patentability search principally investigates prior art to make a preliminary assessment of novelty and inventive step or nonobviousness, but it cannot guarantee grant because unpublished material, search limitations, and legal judgment may affect the result. Patentability also does not establish freedom to operate; a patentable invention may still fall within the scope of another person’s patent.

etymology.ja: patentability は patentable「特許を受け得る」に、性質・能力を表す接尾辞 -ity が付いて成立した。patentable は patent と -able から成る。patent はラテン語 patens「開いている、公にされている」に由来し、patere「開いている」の現在分詞である。君主が公に権利を付与する open letters、すなわち letters patent から、発明について一定期間の排他的権利を与える制度と証書を表すようになった。そこから patentability は、発明がそのような権利付与の法的条件を満たす性質を意味するようになった。
etymology.en: Patentability was formed from patentable with the suffix -ity, which denotes a quality or capacity. Patentable consists of patent and -able. Patent ultimately derives from Latin patens, open or exposed, the present participle of patere, to be open. Letters patent were open official documents through which a sovereign publicly granted rights or privileges. Patent consequently came to denote the document and legal right granting a limited exclusive right in an invention. Patentability then developed as the term for an invention’s capacity to meet the legal conditions for that grant.

usage.uncountable: Prior art is normally uncountable: relevant prior art, not a prior art. For an individual document or disclosure, use a prior-art reference or a piece of prior art.
usage.hyphenation: The expression is normally written without a hyphen as a noun, but is often hyphenated before another noun: prior art and a prior-art search.
usage.legal_scope: Prior art is a legal category whose precise scope and relevant date depend on the applicable patent law and circumstances.
usage.reference: A patent, published application, journal article, product, public use, sale, presentation, or other disclosure may qualify as prior art if the governing legal requirements are satisfied.
usage.patentability: Prior art is principally used in assessing requirements such as novelty and inventive step or nonobviousness.
usage.possessor: The expression does not mean merely information already known personally to the inventor or examiner.

nuance.ja: prior art は単に「以前から存在した技術」を漠然と表すのではなく、特許性判断に利用できる法的な先行技術を指す。ある資料が技術的に古くても、公開時期・公開態様・出願との関係・適用される法域上の例外などによっては、特定の請求項に対する prior art として利用できないことがある。新規性判断では通常、一つの先行技術文献が請求項の全要素を適切に開示しているかが問題となる。一方、進歩性・非自明性では、複数の先行技術を組み合わせる論理や、当業者の知識が検討されることがある。prior art search は関連資料を探す調査であり、その調査で見つかった資料が法的に有効な prior art となるかは別途評価を要する。
nuance.en: Prior art is not merely a loose description of technology that existed earlier; it is a legal category of information capable of being used in a patentability analysis. Technically old material may not qualify against a particular claim because of its publication date, manner of availability, relationship to the application, or an exception under the applicable law. For novelty, the question is generally whether a single prior-art disclosure adequately contains all the required claim elements. Inventive-step or nonobviousness analysis may involve reasoning based on multiple prior-art references and the knowledge of a skilled person. A prior-art search identifies potentially relevant material, but whether each result legally qualifies as prior art requires a separate analysis.

ja: prior art：特許の新規性・進歩性などを判断する際に利用される、法的に適格な既存の技術・開示。
prior-art reference：先行技術として引用・検討される個別の特許文献・論文その他の資料。
state of the art：ある時点における技術水準。文脈や法域によって prior art と重なるが、常に同一ではない。
background art：発明の背景を説明する既存技術。必ずしも法的に適格な先行技術とは限らない。
common general knowledge：関連分野の当業者に一般的に知られている技術知識。
novelty：請求発明が適格な一つの先行開示にすべて示されていないことを求める特許要件。
anticipation：一つの先行技術によって請求発明の全要素が開示され、新規性が否定されること。
prior-art search：発明に関連する先行特許・刊行物・その他の公開情報を探索する調査。
en: prior art is legally qualifying existing technology or disclosure used to assess novelty and inventive step or nonobviousness.
a prior-art reference is an individual patent document, article, or other source considered or cited as prior art.
the state of the art is the level of technological development at a particular time and is not always legally identical to prior art.
background art is existing technology presented to explain an invention’s context and does not necessarily qualify legally as prior art.
common general knowledge is technical knowledge generally possessed by skilled persons in the relevant field.
novelty requires that the claimed invention not be fully disclosed in a qualifying single earlier disclosure.
anticipation occurs when one prior-art disclosure contains every required element of a patent claim.
a prior-art search is an investigation for earlier patents, publications, and other public information relevant to an invention.

etymology.ja: prior はラテン語 prior「前の、より先の」に由来し、art はラテン語 ars「技術、技能」にさかのぼる。特許法における art は美術ではなく、技術・技術分野・技術的知識を意味する。したがって prior art は文字どおりには「先行する技術」であり、発明より前に利用可能であった技術的知識や開示を表す法律用語として定着した。日本語では通常「先行技術」と訳される。
etymology.en: Prior derives from Latin prior, meaning earlier or former, while art ultimately comes from Latin ars, meaning skill or technique. In patent terminology, art does not refer to fine art but to technology, a technical field, or technical knowledge. Prior art therefore literally denotes earlier technology and became established as the legal term for technical information or disclosures available before the relevant date. It is commonly translated into Japanese as 先行技術.

note.ja: 特定時点における技術の到達水準を表す。法的文脈によっては先行技術の総体に近いが、常に同義ではない。
note.en: The level of technological development reached at a particular time; it may overlap with prior art but is not invariably identical.

note.ja: すでに存在する技術を広く表す一般語で、prior art の法的な適格性までは示さない。
note.en: A general expression for technology already in existence, without establishing that it legally qualifies as prior art.

note.ja: 対象となる出願・発明より前に行われた開示を表すが、その開示が先行技術になるかは別途判断を要する。
note.en: A disclosure made earlier than the application or invention, although its legal status as prior art requires further analysis.

note.ja: 明細書などで発明の背景として説明される既存技術で、必ずしも引用可能な先行技術とは限らない。
note.en: Existing technology discussed as background to an invention, which does not necessarily constitute citable prior art.

note.ja: 関連する基準日より前に公表・提供された情報。法的効果は公開状況や適用法によって異なる。
note.en: Information disclosed before the relevant date, whose legal effect depends on its availability and the applicable law.
